slides.kicker: SAVE THESE BEFORE YOU SIGN ANYTHING

slides.headline: 1) PASTE YOUR CONTRACT AND FIND THE TRAPS
slides.body: A contract lawyer charges $350 an hour to review your deal. This is free "Here is my contract. Find every clause that could hurt me and tell me what to change"

slides.headline: 2) READ YOUR LEASE AND FIND HIDDEN COSTS
slides.body: A real estate attorney charges $200 an hour to review a lease. This is free "Here is my lease. Find every clause that could cost me unexpected money and show the section number"

slides.headline: 3) READ YOUR FINE PRINT BEFORE IT COSTS YOU
slides.body: A lawyer charges $250 to read your terms of service. You agree to 150+ a year unread "Here are my terms of service. List the 5 things I'm agreeing to that most people miss"

slides.headline: 4) SCAN YOUR NDA BEFORE YOU SIGN AWAY RIGHTS
slides.body: An IP lawyer charges $400 to review an NDA. Most people just sign and hope "Here is my NDA. Find any clause that limits what I can do after I leave and explain the real-world impact"

slides.headline: 5) CHECK YOUR NON-COMPETE FOR HIDDEN RESTRICTIONS
slides.body: A non-compete review costs $500+ from an employment attorney. This catches what you'd miss "Here is my non-compete agreement. Identify every restriction on where I can work, for how long, and what's enforceable in my state"

slides.headline: 6) GET YOUR JOB OFFER REVIEWED FREE
slides.body: An employment lawyer charges $400 to review a job offer. Most people just sign "Here is my job offer. What am I giving up, what's missing, and what should I negotiate?"

caption:
Swipe to see the six prompts that do what a $350/hour lawyer does, for free 🔐

Contract clause scanner, lease fine-print finder, terms of service decoder, NDA rights checker, non-compete restriction spotter, job offer reviewer: six prompts that do in 30 seconds what costs $200-$500 an hour.

Legal help used to be something only people with money could afford. These prompts don't replace a real lawyer for complex cases, but for everyday contracts, disputes, and fine print, they put everyone on equal ground.

hook_sharpen.why: "Traps in your contracts" is visceral and concrete — I immediately picture something hidden that could hurt me, and I want to know what it is. The lawyer-conspiracy framing of [0] is a tired formula that my brain half-tunes out, while "traps" feels specific and immediate.

editor_override: Hook is a label headline (banned §2) and at 9 words falls below the 12-word minimum — it needs to be ONE complete sentence (12-25 words) with actor + action + the wild specific, e.g. a felt-scale payoff like the total cost saved or the trap count found; All six content slide bodies open with the identical 'A [type] lawyer charges $X / This is free' template — the framing repeats verbatim six times
